subject: Maths
central_question: How can the exposed surface area, volume and capacity of an object made by joining or removing basic solids be calculated correctly?
in_scope_units: Introduction: recognises real objects as combinations of cuboids, cones, cylinders, spheres and hemispheres.
Surface Area of a Combination of Solids: adds only exposed curved or plane surfaces and removes joined or covered faces.
Volume of a Combination of Solids: adds volumes of joined parts and subtracts volumes of cavities, depressions or occupied spaces.
Summary: consolidates methods for surface area and volume of objects formed from basic solids.
banned_topics: Frustums of cones, which are not developed in the supplied chapter.
Similarity-based conversion of one solid into another and melting or recasting problems.
Two-dimensional sector and segment area problems from Areas Related to Circles.
Coordinate geometry or algebraic equations unrelated to mensuration.

known_pitfalls.claim: The total surface area of a joined solid is always the sum of the total surface areas of all its parts.
known_pitfalls.correction: Joined faces become hidden, so only surfaces visible from outside are counted.

known_pitfalls.claim: The volume of joined solids must also exclude their common face.
known_pitfalls.correction: A common face has no volume; volumes of non-overlapping joined parts are added directly.

known_pitfalls.claim: A hemispherical depression reduces surface area because material is removed.
known_pitfalls.correction: For surface area, the removed flat circular part is replaced by the curved surface of the depression; the net effect depends on both areas.

known_pitfalls.claim: The total height of a cone-hemisphere toy is the cone height alone.
known_pitfalls.correction: The cone height equals total height minus the hemisphere radius.

known_pitfalls.claim: Surface area and volume can be calculated using mixed centimetre and metre dimensions.
known_pitfalls.correction: Convert all dimensions to one unit before substitution, then use square units for area and cubic units for volume.

recommended_example_progression: Start with NCERT Figures 12.2–12.5 and NCERT Example 1 to identify constituent solids and exposed curved surfaces.
Use NCERT Examples 2 and 3 to handle hidden attachment areas and a visible circular ring when radii differ.
Use NCERT Example 5 to add volumes of a cuboid and half cylinder and then subtract occupied space.
Use NCERT Example 6 to distinguish apparent capacity from actual capacity when a raised hemisphere occupies space.
Finish with NCERT Exercise 12.2 Question 5 or NCERT Example 7 for subtraction and displacement in a multi-solid volume problem.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: NCERT Exercise 12.1 contains Questions 1–9 on combined surface areas, and Exercise 12.2 contains Questions 1–8 on combined volumes and capacities.
